claims.claim: Two-digit years were used because early computer memory and storage were scarce and expensive, so programs stored only the last two digits of the year.
claims.episode_span: Programmers working with COBOL and FORTRAN on systems for banks, utilities, and government agencies chose to record years as “65” instead of “1965” simply to conserve expensive magnetic tape and core memory.
claims.supporting_quote: programs could simply prefix "19" to the year of a date, allowing them to only store the last two digits of the year instead of four. As space on disc and tape storage was also expensive, these strategies saved money by reducing the size of stored data files and databases

claims.claim: Peter de Jager's widely circulated 1993 Computerworld article 'Doomsday 2000' urged organizations to address the year-2000 problem.
claims.episode_span: Canadian consultant Peter de Jager published widely circulated articles in 1993 urging organizations to begin audits.
claims.supporting_quote: Computerworld ' s 1993 three-page "Doomsday 2000" article by Peter de Jager was called "the information-age equivalent of the midnight ride of Paul Revere " by The New York Times .

claims.claim: In 1998 the United States passed the Year 2000 Information and Readiness Disclosure Act.
claims.episode_span: In 1998 the United States Congress passed the Year 2000 Information and Readiness Disclosure Act
claims.supporting_quote: In 1998, the United States government responded to the Y2K threat by passing the Year 2000 Information and Readiness Disclosure Act, by working with private sector counterparts in order to ensure readiness

claims.claim: The US federal Y2K effort was coordinated by the President's Council on Year 2000 Conversion, headed by John Koskinen.
claims.episode_span: John Koskinen, chair of the President’s Council on Year 2000 Conversion, held weekly televised briefings
claims.supporting_quote: The effort was coordinated by the President's Council on Year 2000 Conversion, headed by John Koskinen , in coordination with the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA)

claims.claim: The total cost of Y2K preparation work likely surpassed US$300 billion.
claims.episode_span: Estimates of global remediation costs, which ranged from $300 billion to $600 billion depending on the study
claims.supporting_quote: The total cost of the work done in preparation for Y2K likely surpassed US$300 billion

claims.claim: The US federal government spent about $8.5 billion on Y2K, within a US total of roughly $100 billion, and worldwide estimates ran to $500-600 billion.
claims.episode_span: the U.S. federal government alone reported spending roughly $8.5 billion on remediation between 1996 and 2000
claims.source_title: Y2K "Crisis" | Computer Science | Research Starters | EBSCO Research
claims.supporting_quote: The United States alone spent $100 billion, including $8.5 billion by the federal government, according to the U.S. Department of Commerce.

claims.claim: The actual transition to the year 2000 passed largely without incident, with most problems minor and easily corrected.
claims.episode_span: When January 1, 2000, arrived, the predicted meltdowns did not materialize.
claims.source_title: Y2K "Crisis" | Computer Science | Research Starters | EBSCO Research
claims.supporting_quote: the actual transition to the year 2000 passed largely without incident. Most problems that did occur were minor and easily corrected
